summary.en: Recognize the six token groups and distinguish C17 keywords from names and C23 additions.
summary.bn: ছয় ধরনের টোকেন চেনো এবং C17 কীওয়ার্ড, নাম ও C23-এর নতুন শব্দ আলাদা করো।

notes: The list of 44 keywords is for C17. C99 and C11 added several of the underscore-prefixed and other modern spellings compared with C90. C23 introduces the additional list above, so code using those additions needs appropriate language mode and implementation support.

examples.title: Tokens in a declaration
examples.explanationHtml: int is a keyword, marks an identifier, 80 a constant, = an operator and ; a punctuator; the format is a string literal.

examples.title: Keyword types, different names
examples.explanationHtml: int keeps its language meaning in both declarations; theory and lab are programmer-chosen identifiers.

examples.title: Punctuation separates expressions
examples.explanationHtml: The comma inside the string is output; commas outside the string separate arguments and are not printed.

examples.title: Mistake: a keyword used as a name
examples.explanationHtml: return has a reserved grammatical role; choose a meaningful non-keyword such as result.

practice.title: Name a score
practice.statementHtml:
Read score 0 to 100; print Input: then score=N and newline.

Write the exact prompt Input: with one space after the colon, then the stated result with its final newline. The input domain is part of the task; no other output is required for these tests.
hints: score is an identifier; int is a keyword.

hints: The 1 token is an integer constant.

practice.statementHtml:

hints: Separate format arguments outside the string too.

hints: Parentheses group the addition before multiplication.

practice.title: A token-rich receipt
practice.statementHtml:
Read count and unit price each 0 to 100; output Input: then count=C, price=P, total=T on separate lines, T=count*price.

Write the exact prompt Input: with one space after the colon, then the stated result with its final newline. The input domain is part of the task; no other output is required for these tests.
hints: The format string is one token even though it contains spaces or escapes.

quiz.prompt: Which token group contains main and marks?
quiz.explanation: These are names; main has a special hosted-program role but is not a keyword.

quiz.prompt: Which spelling is a C17 keyword?
quiz.explanation: while belongs to the language grammar; the other spellings are not C17 keywords.
Spaces inside double quotes belong to the string literal.
A numeric literal is a constant token, even without a named variable.

quiz.prompt: Which became a keyword in C23?
quiz.explanation: C23 adds nullptr; standard library function names do not thereby become keywords.

quiz.prompt: What is bool in C17 after including stdbool.h?
options: A user function defined by main
quiz.explanation: C17 uses _Bool as a keyword and bool as a header macro; C23 changes bool to a keyword.

examQuestions.question: List the six common teaching groups of C tokens and give an example of each.
examQuestions.answerHtml: The groups are keywords such as int, identifiers such as marks, constants such as 80, string literals such as "lab", operators such as +, and other punctuators such as ;. Formally operators belong to the standard punctuator category.

examQuestions.question: Distinguish keywords, library names and macros, including the change in bool between C17 and C23.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
Keywords have fixed grammatical meanings and cannot be reused as ordinary variable names. printf and main are identifiers, although standard names have reservation rules; they are not C17 keywords. A macro is preprocessing substitution. In C17, _Bool is a keyword while stdbool.h provides bool, true and false as macros. C23 makes bool, true and false keywords and adds names such as nullptr and typeof. The selected standard therefore matters when classifying source.

Marking: keyword role 1, identifiers 1, macro role 1, C17 Boolean rule 1, C23 change 1.

examQuestions.question: Write a complete C program for this lab task: Read count and unit price each 0 to 100; output Input: then count=C, price=P, total=T on separate lines, T=count*price.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int count, price;
    printf("Input: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &count, &price) != 2) {
        return 1;
    }
    int total = count * price;
    printf("count=%d\nprice=%d\ntotal=%d\n", count, price, total);
    return 0;
}

Marking: 1 for typed declarations, 1 for checked input, 2 for the required calculation or transformation, and 1 for exact output.
